themes.name: Weekly reorder rebuilt by hand
themes.insight: Both shoppers buy a near-identical basket every week but must search and re-add each item one at a time because there is no reorder or regulars list, turning a 3-minute task into 11+ minutes.

quotes.text: There’s no ‘my regulars’ list, no reorder button. It’s maddening.
I have to search for each item individually. Eggs. Search. Add. Milk. Search. Add. Sourdough. Search. Add. And so on. Every. Single. Week.
I timed it last Sunday. Eleven minutes. Eleven minutes to order essentially the same things I ordered the week before.

themes.name: Silent substitutions with no control
themes.insight: Out-of-stock items are swapped without warning and with no accept/reject or alternative-picking step, so shoppers only discover the wrong item on delivery — an experience that has already driven cancellation.

quotes.text: And nobody told me. No text, no email, no ‘hey, we’re out of thighs, is this OK?’ It just arrived wrong.
Don’t silently swap my food and hope I won’t notice. I’m not an idiot.
One more bad experience and I’m done. I don’t have the bandwidth.

themes.name: Storefront with no editorial layer
themes.insight: The browse experience is an unsorted product grid with no seasonality, curation, or producer stories, so the exploration-minded shopper falls back to search-only and keeps checking the unchanged homepage hoping for something new.

quotes.text: it was like someone had built a gorgeous storefront and then put a spreadsheet inside it.
Number one, by a mile, is product discovery. The browsing experience.
Search. Honestly, search is the only reliable way.

themes.name: Delivery timing left unsaid
themes.insight: Shoppers accept the two-day delivery speed but not the opacity around it — a day-only window and no proactive update when an order slips break meal planning and household logistics.

quotes.text: It’s the silence that’s frustrating, not the speed.
I was tracking it and there was no update for, like, 36 hours. I didn’t know if it was lost or just delayed.
‘Monday’ isn’t a delivery window. I need to know if it’s morning or afternoon because Kate works Tuesdays

themes.name: Impact Score means nothing
themes.insight: The sustainability number carries no context or breakdown, so one shopper can't tell if her score is good and the other ignores it entirely; both want a tangible per-order outcome instead (farms supported, waste prevented, food miles).

quotes.text: I don’t really know what a 73 means. Like, is that good? Out of what? What would an 80 look like versus a 60? There’s no context.
A number out of a hundred doesn’t make me feel anything.
tell me— ‘Mark, your orders this month supported four local farms and saved the equivalent of planting three trees.’

themes.name: GreenBasket is the side shop
themes.insight: Because staples and range are thin, both shoppers give the bulk of their grocery spend to Ocado/Sainsbury's/Abel & Cole and treat GreenBasket as a top-up for veg and bakery, despite rating its product quality highest.

quotes.text: If GreenBasket had, like, two hundred more SKUs in the staples category, I’d probably consolidate.
Sainsbury’s for the boring stuff. Pasta, tinned tomatoes, cleaning products. The stuff that GreenBasket just doesn’t have yet.
And then GreenBasket is sort of— the supplementary thing. Fresh veg, meat sometimes, the bakery stuff.

gaps: Only two participants, both London-based professionals (31 and 45) who kept using GreenBasket — no churned/lapsed users, no non-users, no rural or non-London shoppers, no students or older shoppers.

Direct tension the corpus can't resolve: editorial/discovery browsing is Sarah's #1 want but Mark explicitly rejects it ("I don’t need a beautiful discovery experience") — unknown which segment is larger.
All behaviour is self-reported recall; no observed sessions, so time estimates (11 min, 36 hours) and flow friction points are unverified.
No data on GreenBasket's actual SKU count, delivery SLA, or substitution rate — pains are reported but their scale and root cause are unknown.
Whether the Impact Score is designed to expand on tap, and what its methodology is, is unknown.
No signal on price sensitivity or willingness to pay more for these fixes; both value quality but neither was asked about price.
Mobile vs desktop ordering UX for GreenBasket specifically is unexplored, though one spouse reportedly avoids phone ordering.
